solution:
The class is fixed by what the halogen-bearing carbon is attached to: alkyl (\(\text{sp}^3\) carbon, further labelled 1\(^\circ\)/2\(^\circ\)/3\(^\circ\) by how many carbons that carbon carries), vinylic (halogen on a doubly-bonded carbon), allylic (on the carbon next to a double bond), benzylic (on a carbon attached to a ring) or aryl (halogen on the ring itself).

(i) 2-Chloro-3-methylbutane — secondary (2\(^\circ\)) alkyl halide

(ii) 3-Chloro-4-methylhexane — secondary (2\(^\circ\)) alkyl halide

(iii) 1-Iodo-2,2-dimethylbutane — primary (1\(^\circ\)) alkyl halide

(iv) 1-Bromo-3,3-dimethyl-1-phenylbutane — secondary (2\(^\circ\)) benzylic halide

(v) 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane — secondary (2\(^\circ\)) alkyl halide

(vi) 1-Bromo-2-ethyl-2-methylbutane — primary (1\(^\circ\)) alkyl halide

(vii) 3-Chloro-3-methylpentane — tertiary (3\(^\circ\)) alkyl halide

(viii) 3-Chloro-5-methylhex-2-ene — vinylic halide (the chlorine is on a doubly-bonded carbon)

(ix) 4-Bromo-4-methylpent-2-ene — tertiary allylic halide (the bromine is on the carbon next to the double bond)

(x) 1-Chloro-4-(2-methylpropyl)benzene — aryl halide

(xi) 1-(Chloromethyl)-3-(2,2-dimethylpropyl)benzene — primary (1\(^\circ\)) benzylic halide

(xii) 1-Bromo-2-(1-methylpropyl)benzene — aryl halide

(i) 2-Bromo-3-chlorobutane. Butane chain; the locant set \(\{2,3\}\) is the same from either end, so the tie is broken alphabetically and bromo takes the lower number.

(ii) 1-Bromo-1-chloro-1,2,2-trifluoroethane. Numbering from the \(\text{CBrClF}\) carbon gives locants \(\{1,1,1,2,2\}\), lower than \(\{1,1,2,2,2\}\) from the other end.

(iii) 1-Bromo-4-chlorobut-2-yne.

(iv) 1,1,1,2,3,3,3-Heptachloro-2-(trichloromethyl)propane. The parent is the three-carbon chain \(\text{CCl}_3-\text{CCl}(-)-\text{CCl}_3\), leaving the fourth \(\text{CCl}_3\) as a substituent on C-2.

(v) 3-Bromo-2,2-bis(4-chlorophenyl)butane. Numbering from the end nearer the two aryl groups gives \(\{2,2,3\}\), which beats \(\{2,3,3\}\).

(vi) 1-Chloro-1-(4-iodophenyl)-3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene.

(i) 2-Chloro-3-methylpentane: \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{Cl})\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\)

(ii) \(p\)-Bromochlorobenzene: a benzene ring with \(\text{Br}\) and \(\text{Cl}\) on opposite (1,4) carbons — \(\text{BrC}_6\text{H}_4\text{Cl}\)

(iii) 1-Chloro-4-ethylcyclohexane: a cyclohexane ring with \(\text{Cl}\) at C-1 and \(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\) at C-4

(iv) 2-(2-Chlorophenyl)-1-iodooctane: an eight-carbon chain with \(\text{I}\) on C-1 and an \(o\)-chlorophenyl ring on C-2 — \(\text{ICH}_2\text{CH}(\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{Cl})\text{CH}_2(\text{CH}_2)_4\text{CH}_3\)

(v) 2-Bromobutane: \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\)

(vi) 4-tert-Butyl-3-iodoheptane: \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{I})\text{CH}[\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_3]\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\)

(vii) 1-Bromo-4-sec-butyl-2-methylbenzene: a benzene ring with \(\text{Br}\) at C-1, \(\text{CH}_3\) at C-2 and \(-\text{CH}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\) at C-4

(viii) 1,4-Dibromobut-2-ene: \(\text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_2\text{Br}\)

Dichloromethane, \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2\), has the highest dipole moment.

The molecular dipole is the vector sum of the individual bond moments in a tetrahedral molecule. In \(\text{CCl}_4\) the four identical \(\text{C}-\text{Cl}\) moments point to the corners of a regular tetrahedron and cancel exactly, so \(\mu = 0\). In \(\text{CHCl}_3\) the resultant of two of the \(\text{C}-\text{Cl}\) moments is directed against the third, which cuts the total down. In \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2\) there are only two \(\text{C}-\text{Cl}\) moments and their resultant is reinforced rather than opposed, giving the largest net moment.

Measured values bear this out: \(\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2\) about \(1.60\,\text{D}\), \(\text{CHCl}_3\) about \(1.08\,\text{D}\), \(\text{CCl}_4\) exactly zero.

The hydrocarbon is cyclopentane.

Two clues fix it. \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\) has one degree of unsaturation, so it is either an alkene or a ring; but it does NOT react with chlorine in the dark, and an alkene would add chlorine readily in the dark, so it must be a ring — a cycloalkane. In bright sunlight it undergoes free-radical substitution instead, and it gives only ONE monochloro product, which means all its hydrogen atoms are equivalent.

Of the cyclopentane and methylcyclobutane type structures only cyclopentane has all ten hydrogens equivalent, so it gives the single product chlorocyclopentane, \(\text{C}_5\text{H}_9\text{Cl}\).

The hydrocarbon is cyclopentane.

\(\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{Br}\) has four isomers — two from the straight chain and two from the branched chain:

\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}\) — 1-bromobutane (1\(^\circ\))

\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_3\) — 2-bromobutane (2\(^\circ\))

\((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCH}_2\text{Br}\) — 1-bromo-2-methylpropane (1\(^\circ\))

\((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CBr}\) — 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (3\(^\circ\))

(i) From 1-butanol — treat with \(\text{NaI}\) in the presence of \(\text{H}_3\text{PO}_4\) (a non-oxidising acid, so the \(\text{HI}\) generated is not destroyed):
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH} + \text{NaI} + \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{I} + \text{NaH}_2\text{PO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)

(ii) From 1-chlorobutane — the Finkelstein reaction with \(\text{NaI}\) in dry acetone, which works because \(\text{NaCl}\) is insoluble in acetone and precipitates, pulling the equilibrium over:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{NaI} \xrightarrow{\text{dry acetone}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{I} + \text{NaCl}\)

(iii) From but-1-ene — two steps are needed, because the iodine must end up on the TERMINAL carbon and direct addition of \(\text{HI}\) would follow Markovnikov's rule and give 2-iodobutane. Only \(\text{HBr}\) shows the peroxide effect, so add \(\text{HBr}\) in the presence of peroxide to place the halogen at C-1, then exchange it for iodine:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 + \text{HBr} \xrightarrow{\text{peroxide}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}\)
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{NaI} \xrightarrow{\text{dry acetone}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{I} + \text{NaBr}\)

An ambident nucleophile is a nucleophile that has TWO different donor atoms through either of which it can attack, so it can give two different products depending on which end does the attacking.

Example — the cyanide ion, \([\text{C}\equiv\text{N}]^-\), which is a resonance hybrid with lone pairs available on both carbon and nitrogen. Attack through carbon gives an alkyl cyanide, and attack through nitrogen gives an alkyl isocyanide:
\(\text{R}-\text{X} + \text{KCN} \rightarrow \text{R}-\text{CN}\) (alkyl cyanide, the main product with the ionic \(\text{KCN}\))
\(\text{R}-\text{X} + \text{AgCN} \rightarrow \text{R}-\text{NC}\) (alkyl isocyanide, the main product with the largely covalent \(\text{AgCN}\))

The nitrite ion is ambident in the same way, giving alkyl nitrites \(\text{R}-\text{O}-\text{N}=\text{O}\) through oxygen and nitroalkanes \(\text{R}-\text{NO}_2\) through nitrogen.

(i) \(\text{CH}_3\text{I}\) reacts faster. The two compounds differ only in the halogen, so the comparison is one of leaving-group ability: iodide is the larger, more polarisable ion and the weaker base, and the \(\text{C}-\text{I}\) bond is the weakest of the carbon-halogen bonds, so it breaks most readily.

(ii) \(\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}\) reacts faster. Here the halogen is the same and the comparison is steric: the methyl carbon carries only hydrogen atoms and is wide open to backside attack, whereas the three bulky methyl groups of \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCl}\) shield its carbon almost completely from the incoming hydroxide ion.

Sodium ethoxide in ethanol removes a \(\beta\)-hydrogen and the halogen to give an alkene. Where different \(\beta\)-carbons are available, different alkenes result, and by Saytzeff's rule the major product is the more highly substituted (hence more stable) alkene.

(i) 1-Bromo-1-methylcyclohexane — the \(\beta\)-hydrogens lie either on a ring carbon or on the methyl group:
1-methylcyclohexene (trisubstituted, from the ring \(\beta\)-hydrogen) and methylenecyclohexane (disubstituted, from the methyl).
Major: 1-methylcyclohexene.

(ii) 2-Chloro-2-methylbutane, \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}(\text{Cl})\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\) — the \(\beta\)-hydrogens lie on the two methyl groups or on the \(\text{CH}_2\):
2-methylbut-2-ene, \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}=\text{CHCH}_3\) (trisubstituted) and 2-methylbut-1-ene, \(\text{CH}_2=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\) (disubstituted).
Major: 2-methylbut-2-ene.

(iii) 2,2,3-Trimethyl-3-bromopentane, \(\text{CH}_3\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{C}(\text{Br})(\text{CH}_3)\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\) — note that one neighbouring carbon is quaternary and has NO hydrogen, so elimination can only go towards the \(\text{CH}_2\) group or towards the methyl on the same carbon:
3,4,4-trimethylpent-2-ene, \(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_3\) (trisubstituted) and 2-ethyl-3,3-dimethylbut-1-ene, \(\text{CH}_2=\text{C}(\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3)\text{C}(\text{CH}_3)_3\) (disubstituted).
Major: 3,4,4-trimethylpent-2-ene.

(i) Ethanol to but-1-yne:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{conc. H}_2\text{SO}_4,\ 443\,\text{K}} \text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2/\text{CCl}_4} \text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KOH, then NaNH}_2} \text{HC}\equiv\text{CH}\)
then \(\text{HC}\equiv\text{CH} \xrightarrow{\text{NaNH}_2} \text{HC}\equiv\text{C}^-\text{Na}^+ \xrightarrow{\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Br}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{CH}\)

(ii) Ethane to bromoethene:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2,\ \text{UV light}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KOH}} \text{CH}_2=\text{CH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2/\text{CCl}_4} \text{BrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KOH (1 mol)}} \text{CH}_2=\text{CHBr}\)

(iii) Propene to 1-nitropropane — the peroxide effect is needed to put the halogen on the terminal carbon:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{HBr, peroxide}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{AgNO}_2} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NO}_2\)

(iv) Toluene to benzyl alcohol — chlorination in sunlight attacks the side chain, not the ring:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{Cl}_2,\ \text{UV light}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{aq. NaOH}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\)

(v) Propene to propyne:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2/\text{CCl}_4} \text{CH}_3\text{CHBrCH}_2\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KOH, then NaNH}_2} \text{CH}_3\text{C}\equiv\text{CH}\)

(vi) Ethanol to ethyl fluoride — by the Swarts reaction, since fluorides are best made by halogen exchange:
\(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{PCl}_5} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{AgF or Hg}_2\text{F}_2} \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{F}\)

(vii) Bromomethane to propanone — the nitrile supplies the second carbon and the Grignard the third:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KCN}} \text{CH}_3\text{CN} \xrightarrow{\text{(1) CH}_3\text{MgBr};\ \text{(2) H}_3\text{O}^+} \text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3\)

(viii) But-1-ene to but-2-ene — add \(\text{HBr}\) by Markovnikov's rule (no peroxide) so the bromine goes to C-2, then eliminate:
\(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}=\text{CH}_2 \xrightarrow{\text{HBr}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}(\text{Br})\text{CH}_3 \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KOH}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3\)

(ix) 1-Chlorobutane to n-octane — the Wurtz reaction joins two identical alkyl groups:
\(2\,\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + 2\text{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_6\text{CH}_3 + 2\text{NaCl}\)

(x) Benzene to biphenyl — the Fittig reaction is the aryl analogue of Wurtz:
\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_6 \xrightarrow{\text{Cl}_2,\ \text{anhyd. AlCl}_3} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl}\), then \(2\,\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + 2\text{Na} \xrightarrow{\text{dry ether}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{C}_6\text{H}_5 + 2\text{NaCl}\)
